concepts.name: What is a volcano?
facts: A volcano is an opening in Earth's crust.
Hot melted rock can escape through a volcano.
Many volcanoes are shaped like mountains.

concepts.name: Inside a volcano
facts: Melted rock under the ground is called magma.
Magma that flows out onto the surface is called lava.
A crater is a bowl-shaped hollow at the top.

concepts.name: Eruptions
facts: Lava cools and hardens into new rock.
Ash and gas can shoot high into the sky.
Scientists watch volcanoes to warn people.

concepts.name: Famous volcanoes
facts: Mount Fuji is a famous volcano in Japan.
Many volcanoes lie around the Pacific, in the Ring of Fire.
The islands of Hawaii were built by volcanoes.

questions.prompt: What is a volcano?
questions.hint: Think of fire and rock coming out of a mountain.
questions.explanation: A volcano is an opening in Earth's crust where hot melted rock, ash and gas can escape.

questions.prompt: What comes out of a volcano when it erupts?
questions.hint: It is very hot.
questions.explanation: An erupting volcano can throw out lava, ash and gases.

questions.prompt: Which shape do many volcanoes have?
questions.hint: Think of a pointed hill.
questions.explanation: Many volcanoes are cone-shaped mountains built from layers of lava and ash.

questions.prompt: How do volcanoes build mountains?
questions.hint: Think about what is left after each eruption.
questions.explanation: Each eruption adds layers of lava and ash. Over time the layers build a mountain.

questions.prompt: What is an active volcano?
questions.hint: It is not asleep.
questions.explanation: An active volcano has erupted recently or may erupt again. A dormant one is asleep but could wake up.

questions.prompt: A volcano that will probably never erupt again is called what?
questions.hint: Like animals that have died out.
questions.explanation: An extinct volcano is one that scientists think will not erupt again.

questions.prompt: Why are many volcanoes found at the edges of plates?
questions.hint: Earth's crust is broken into big pieces.
questions.explanation: Earth's crust is split into plates. At their edges there are cracks and gaps where magma can rise.

questions.prompt: A volcano is always a tall mountain.
questions.hint: Not every volcano looks the same.
questions.explanation: Some volcanoes are low hills, flat openings in the ground, or hidden under the sea.

questions.prompt: Lava is very hot.
questions.hint: Think about what can melt rock.
questions.explanation: Lava is melted rock hotter than 700 degrees Celsius, hot enough to burn almost anything.

questions.prompt: Volcanoes can be found under the sea.
questions.hint: Think about volcanic islands.
questions.explanation: Many volcanoes are on the ocean floor, and some of them grow tall enough to make islands.

questions.prompt: How does a volcano build a mountain? Choose each next step.
questions.hint: Think about what happens after lava stops flowing.
questions.explanation: Magma rises and erupts as lava. The lava cools into rock, and layer after layer builds a mountain.

questions.prompt: Put the layers of Earth in order, from the surface down.
questions.hint: The crust is the layer we live on.
questions.explanation: Earth's layers from the top are the crust, the mantle, the liquid outer core and the solid inner core.

questions.prompt: What is melted rock under the ground called?
questions.hint: It sits deep below the surface.
questions.explanation: Melted rock underground is called magma. When it reaches the surface it is called lava.

questions.prompt: What is melted rock called after it flows out of a volcano?
questions.hint: It is on the surface now.
questions.explanation: Magma that reaches Earth's surface is called lava.

questions.prompt: What is the bowl-shaped hollow at the top of a volcano?
questions.hint: Think of a big bowl.
questions.explanation: The crater is a bowl-shaped hollow at the top of a volcano where material comes out.

questions.prompt: What is the long pipe that magma rises through?
questions.hint: Think of a pipe or chimney.
questions.explanation: Magma rises through a long pipe called the vent and leaves the volcano through the crater.

questions.prompt: Where does magma collect before an eruption?
questions.hint: It is deep underground.
questions.explanation: Magma gathers in a big underground pocket called the magma chamber.

questions.prompt: Why does magma rise up through the crust?
questions.hint: Think about what floats in water.
questions.explanation: Magma is less dense than the solid rock around it, so it slowly rises.

questions.prompt: Magma is found under the ground.
questions.hint: Think about where it is before it erupts.
questions.explanation: Magma is melted rock that sits underground. It is called lava once it reaches the surface.

questions.prompt: Lava is liquid rock on the surface.
questions.hint: Think about what flows down the side.
questions.explanation: Lava is magma that has reached the surface, and it flows as a hot liquid.

questions.prompt: A volcano's crater is at the bottom of the volcano.
questions.hint: Think about the shape of a bowl.
questions.explanation: The crater is the bowl-shaped hollow at the top of a volcano.

questions.prompt: Gas trapped in magma helps cause eruptions.
questions.hint: Think about a shaken fizzy drink.
questions.explanation: Gas dissolved in magma expands as the magma rises, and that pushes the magma out in an eruption.

questions.prompt: Why does magma rise up? Choose each next step.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to light things in water.
questions.explanation: Magma is less dense than the rock around it. It rises through cracks, and pressure builds up as more magma gathers.

questions.prompt: Put these in order, from deep underground up to the sky.
questions.hint: Start deep in the ground and end in the air.
questions.explanation: Magma waits in the chamber, rises through the vent, leaves through the crater and can form an ash cloud above.

questions.prompt: What do we call a volcano blowing out lava and ash?
questions.hint: A volcano does this when it wakes up.
questions.explanation: When a volcano blows out lava, ash and gas, that is called an eruption.

questions.prompt: What happens to lava as it cools?
questions.hint: Think about the shape it takes when it stops.
questions.explanation: As lava cools it turns solid and forms new rock.

questions.prompt: Which of these can fly out of a volcano and fill the sky?
questions.hint: It can turn the sky dark.
questions.explanation: Eruptions can shoot ash and gas high into the air, where they can form big dark clouds.

questions.prompt: How do scientists help keep people safe near volcanoes?
questions.hint: They use special instruments.
questions.explanation: Scientists watch for small earthquakes, gas and swelling ground, and warn people before an eruption.

questions.prompt: Why do some farmers like to live near volcanoes?
questions.hint: Think about growing crops.
questions.explanation: Volcanic ash breaks down into soil full of minerals, which helps plants grow well.

questions.prompt: What is a fast cloud of hot gas and ash on a volcano called?
questions.hint: It rushes down the side like an avalanche.
questions.explanation: A pyroclastic flow is a fast, very hot avalanche of gas, ash and rock. It is one of the most dangerous volcano hazards.

questions.prompt: All volcanoes erupt with a huge explosion.
questions.hint: Some volcanoes ooze lava slowly.
questions.explanation: Some volcanoes explode, but others let runny lava flow out gently.

questions.prompt: Lava hardens into rock when it cools.
questions.hint: Think about what happens when something hot cools down.
questions.explanation: Lava turns into solid rock as it cools.

questions.prompt: Volcanic ash is made of tiny bits of rock and glass.
questions.hint: It is not like ash from a campfire.
questions.explanation: Volcanic ash is made of tiny, sharp pieces of rock and glass, not burnt wood.

questions.prompt: A big eruption can change the weather around the world.
questions.hint: Think about ash blocking the Sun.
questions.explanation: Big eruptions throw ash and gas high into the sky. This can block sunlight and cool Earth for a while.

questions.prompt: Why does a volcano erupt? Choose each next step.
questions.hint: Think about opening a shaken fizzy drink.
questions.explanation: Gas is trapped in magma. As the magma rises, pressure drops and the gas bubbles expand and push the magma out.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of an eruption in order.
questions.hint: The eruption comes before the lava cools.
questions.explanation: Magma rises and pressure builds. Then the volcano erupts, and finally the lava cools into rock.

questions.prompt: In which country is Mount Fuji?
questions.hint: It is an island country in Asia.
questions.explanation: Mount Fuji is Japan's highest mountain and a famous volcano.

questions.prompt: Where is the Ring of Fire?
questions.hint: It circles the biggest ocean.
questions.explanation: The Ring of Fire is a horseshoe of volcanoes and earthquakes around the Pacific Ocean.

questions.prompt: Which of these islands were built by volcanoes?
questions.hint: It is in the middle of the Pacific Ocean.
questions.explanation: The Hawaiian islands were built by volcanoes rising from the sea floor.

questions.prompt: Which volcano buried the Roman town of Pompeii?
questions.hint: It is in Italy, near Naples.
questions.explanation: Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE and buried Pompeii under ash.

questions.prompt: Which country has many volcanoes and geysers?
questions.hint: It is a cold island in the north Atlantic.
questions.explanation: Iceland sits on a crack in the sea floor, so it has many volcanoes, hot springs and geysers.

questions.prompt: Why is Mauna Loa in Hawaii called a shield volcano?
questions.hint: Picture a shield lying flat on the ground.
questions.explanation: Shield volcanoes have wide, gently sloping sides built by runny lava, like a warrior's shield lying flat.

questions.prompt: The Hawaiian islands were built by volcanoes.
questions.hint: Think about how an island can rise from the sea.
questions.explanation: Hawaii's islands grew from volcanoes that rose from the ocean floor.

questions.prompt: Mount Fuji is in Italy.
questions.hint: Think about the country with cherry blossoms.
questions.explanation: Mount Fuji is in Japan, not Italy.

questions.prompt: Mount Vesuvius is a volcano in Italy.
questions.hint: Think about Pompeii.
questions.explanation: Vesuvius is a volcano near Naples in Italy.

questions.prompt: There are no volcanoes in Antarctica.
questions.hint: Even the coldest places can have them.
questions.explanation: Antarctica has volcanoes, such as Mount Erebus, which has a lava lake.

questions.prompt: Mount Fuji is 3,776 m tall. A hill is 1,000 m. How much taller is Fuji?
questions.hint: How much more means subtract.
questions.explanation: 3,776 - 1,000 = 2,776, so Mount Fuji is 2,776 m taller than the hill.

questions.prompt: Put these eruptions in order, earliest first.
questions.hint: They run from 79 CE to 2010.
questions.explanation: Vesuvius buried Pompeii in 79 CE, Krakatoa erupted in 1883, Mount St. Helens in 1980 and an Icelandic volcano sent up an ash cloud in 2010.

questions.prompt: Step only on things that can come out of a volcano.
questions.hint: Think of what an eruption looks like.
questions.explanation: Volcanoes throw out lava, ash, gas, rocks and steam. Fish, ice cream, pizza, teddy bears and soap bubbles do not come out of a volcano.

questions.prompt: Step only on parts of a volcano.
questions.hint: A volcano has a chamber, a pipe and a top.
questions.explanation: A volcano has a magma chamber below, a vent that carries magma up, a cone and a crater at the top. The others are parts of machines.

questions.prompt: Step only on warning signs of an eruption.
questions.hint: Scientists measure the ground and the gas.
questions.explanation: Before an eruption the ground shakes, swells and heats up, and more gas and steam escape. The moon, birds, wind and snow tell us nothing about it.

questions.prompt: Step only on volcanoes.
questions.hint: Some mountains are volcanoes and some are not.
questions.explanation: Mount Fuji, Vesuvius, Etna, Krakatoa and Mount St. Helens are volcanoes. Everest, K2, Mont Blanc, the Matterhorn and Table Mountain were pushed up or carved by other forces.
